claims.text: In a single-phase HEA outside traditional Nb-Ta and Ti-rich heavy-transition-metal systems, Tc is primarily governed by atomic-scale lattice distortion.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch among the constituent elements increases lattice distortion.
Moderate lattice distortion softens selected phonon modes.
Softening selected phonon modes enhances the electron-phonon coupling constant.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling facilitates Cooper-pair formation and raises Tc.
Scattering generated by excessive distortion acts as a Cooper-pair breaker and suppresses Tc.
Progressively increasing atomic-size mismatch will produce a non-monotonic Tc response: an initial increase, an optimum, and then a decline.
Local bond-length variations and XRD peak broadening can be used to quantify the degree of lattice distortion.
Holding average valence-electron count nearly constant while preserving the same single-phase BCC structure provides a controlled comparison of lattice-distortion effects.
The proposed baseline is an equiatomic, single-phase BCC HEA with moderate atomic-size mismatch and a superconducting transition at Tc0.
The hypothesis applies only while the alloys remain homogeneous single-phase solid solutions with at least five constituents, each at no less than 5 at.%.
The relevant superconducting temperature range is assumed to be below approximately 20 K.
Short-range ordering may modify electron-phonon coupling and complicate the relationship between lattice distortion and Tc.
Failure to observe the predicted non-monotonic Tc response in a phase-matched composition series would falsify the hypothesis.
